summary: Defines a new DHCPv6 Unique Identifier type, DUID-UUID, derived from the standard UUID format. Devices can use their UUIDs to identify themselves to DHCP servers and vice versa, since UUIDs are globally unique and readily available on many systems.

plainLanguage.summary: DUID-UUID lets a DHCPv6 client or server use a persistent UUID as its DHCP identifier. The UUID must remain available across the system's boot stages that use DHCP.

questions: how is a duid uuid formatted
what uuid should be used for dhcpv6
subtitle: A DHCPv6 unique identifier made from a UUID.

tldr.problem: Some multi-stage network boot processes need every stage to identify the same device to DHCP, while existing DUID types may vary across stages.
tldr.mechanism: DUID-UUID has DUID type 4 followed by a 128-bit UUID that must persist and be available to DHCP agents.
tldr.outcome: The identifier provides another DUID choice, but implementations must ensure boot stages actually use the same value.

today: RFC 6355 is a Proposed Standard. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why Add a UUID-Based Identifier
sections.content:
DHCPv6 uses DUIDs to identify clients and servers. During multi-step network boot, several stages may invoke DHCP, and some environments need each stage to use the same DUID so the server recognizes one device and returns appropriate configuration.

Existing link-layer DUIDs may vary with the chosen interface or timestamp. The RFC defines DUID-UUID, while noting that defining the type alone does not ensure every boot stage selects the same identifier.
sections.plainLanguage: A device may request network configuration several times as it boots. A persistent UUID can help each stage identify the same device.

sections.title: DUID-UUID Format
sections.content:
DUID-UUID appears in a Client Identifier or Server Identifier option. It consists of the DUID type field with value 4, followed by a 128-bit UUID.

The UUID should persist across restarts and reconfiguration and be available to all DHCP agents that need it. The RFC gives a UUID in system firmware as an example of a suitable source.
sections.plainLanguage: The format contains a type number and the UUID. The system must be able to provide the same UUID to the DHCP stages that need it.

sections.title: Assignment and Privacy
sections.content:
IANA assigned DUID type value 4 to DUID-UUID. The RFC says not all UUIDs meet DHCP's persistence and availability requirements.

DHCP traffic is sent in the clear, so an eavesdropper on the path can see a device's UUID. The RFC says this may raise privacy issues but is not a new issue introduced by this DUID type.
sections.plainLanguage: Choose a UUID that stays available and stable. Because DHCP traffic is visible on the path, an observer may learn the identifier.
